{"url": "https://api.crossref.org/works?query=decision-theoretic+foundations+of+temporal+persistence+and+instrumental+convergence+of+goals+across+agent+invocations&rows=4&select=DOI%2Ctitle%2Cabstract%2CURL%2Cpublished", "scope": "Crossref bibliographic metadata and abstracts where supplied; not full papers", "excerpt": "[{\"DOI\": \"10.21236/ada567155\", \"title\": [\"Decision-Theoretic Foundations for Multi-Agent Systems\"], \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.21236/ada567155\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2011, 12, 23]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.21203/rs.3.rs-11137330/v1\", \"title\": [\"Designing an Ethical Framework for Multi-Agent AI Negotiation in Hospital Clinical Decision Support Systems: From Game-Theoretic Foundations to Novel Musical Chairs Coalition Convergence Game (MC3G)\"], \"abstract\": \"Abstract\\n

Agentic AI systems are increasingly deployed in hospitals clinical decision support systems (CDSS), where multiple specialized agents negotiate over patient-care recommendations. This distributed negotiation introduced as “many hands” problem: overrides, disagreements and consensus-building can become opaque, and responsibility for erroneous outcomes cannot be clearly attributed. Existing healthcare AI ethics guidance largely address single system, output facing behavior and does not formally govern internal multi-agent negotiation. This study first synthesizes nine established game theoretic and mechanism design paradigms-including Prisoner's Dilemma, Bayesian games, signaling games, principal-agent theory, Stag Hunt, repeated games, VCG style mechanism design, Shapley value, and Chicken/Hawk-Dove mapping: their applicability and limitations for ethically accountable multi-agent CDSS negotiation. Building on this synthesis, we purpose the Musical Chairs Coalition Convergence Game (MC3G), a novel coalition-based framework that governs agent negotiation with a bounded protocol clock, a reputation-weighted convergence rule, and a mandatory escalation-to-human safety valve for any agent that fails to converge. As a proof-of-concept illustration of the framework’s qualitative behaviour rather than a clinically validated evaluation, we ran a synthetic simulation, non-inferential toy simulation (four agents, 2,000 cases per condition, varying strategic agent prevalence) comparing MC3G against naïve majority voting and reputation-only baseline. In this synthetic setting MC3G showed a lower silent failure rate alongside a higher human escalation rate, converting some undetected errors into flagged reviews. This offers a formally grounded, safety-first architecture for accountable multi-agent clinical decision-making, motivating future evaluation with real agents and data.

\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.21203/rs.3.rs-11137330/v1\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026, 9, 24]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.2307/j.ctvjsf522.4\", \"title\": [\"Decision-Theoretic Foundations\"], \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2307/j.ctvjsf522.4\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2013, 3, 1]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.7584879\", \"title\": [\"The normative foundations of AI regulation in North America, Europe, Russia, and China: Instrumental convergence without normative convergence\"], \"abstract\": \"The global race over Artificial Intelligence (AI) has triggered a parallel competition over regulation. Major economies are competing to shape global AI governance norms and export their values either through horizontal regulations, as the European Union does, or by 'lighttouch' intervention to foster innovation, an approach favoured by the United States and the United Kingdom. This article conducts a comparative analysis of European (European Union (EU) and United Kingdom), North American (U.S. and Canada), Russian, and Chinese policies on AI. My paper aims to answer the following question: what are the normative and philosophical foundations underlying these distinctive models of AI regulation and how is geopolitical competition affecting these models? To answer this question, I survey policy and legal documents adopted between 2016 and 2026 across six jurisdictions. My corpus includes hard law, soft law, and national strategies; supplemented by officials' public declarations. The article identifies three normative traditions: rights-based tempered by utilitarianism (EU and Canada), pragmatic-utilitarian (U.S. and UK), and collectivist (Russia and China). The central empirical finding is that there has been a rhetorical convergence towards the European model between 2019 and 2023. From 2023 until 2026, geopolitical competition has produced what I term 'instrumental convergence' towards a market-based framework, despite no normative consensus. The three models increasingly share regulatory features which obscure persisting differences in underlying values. This article makes three contributions. First, I provide an extended summary of AI policies in six countries and their evolution over time. Second, I provide a normative typology of the major AI regulatory models beyond legal instruments. Third, I document rhetorical and instrumental convergences in AI regulations, advancing hypotheses for this phenomenon. This paper aims to provide insights for policymakers and for the design of multilateral AI governance frameworks, such as those developed within the ITU, at UNESCO or the OECD. I conclude by arguing in favour of a regime of international treaties over technical harmonisation (ISO and other norms) to solve cooperation issues amid conflicting normative models. Report on AI use: Artificial intelligence tools were used at various stages of the research, such as when searching institutional literature.
